slides.title: Purpose and principle
bullets: Platelets are non-nucleated cells 2–4 µm in diameter; they take part in haemostasis and blood clotting.
Ways of counting platelets: the Fonio method, counting in a Goryaev chamber and an automatic haematology analyser.
In the Fonio method platelets are counted in a blood smear against 1000 red cells and then multiplied by the red-cell count per litre of blood.
The reference interval differs between sources and laboratories (MSD Manual: 140–440 × 10⁹/L) — use the interval on the laboratory report form.

slides.title: Procedure
bullets: 1. Draw 14% magnesium sulfate or 6% EDTA solution into a Panchenkov capillary up to the “25” mark and expel it into a tube.
2. Draw blood from the finger into the Panchenkov capillary up to the K mark and add it to the tube.
3. Mix the tube well, make a smear from it, fix it and stain it by Romanowsky–Giemsa.
4. At 1000× magnification (immersion) count the platelets against 1000 red cells (‰).
5. Knowing the red-cell count per µL of blood, calculate the platelet count per litre.

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: Platelets (× 10⁹/L) = red cells (× 10¹²/L) × the number of platelets per 1000 red cells.
Normal by the Fonio method: 45–70 ‰ against 1000 red cells.
Thrombocytopenia is a fall, and thrombocytosis a rise, of the platelet count outside the reference interval.
Thrombocytosis may be reactive (secondary — e.g. in inflammation or blood loss) or primary (a bone-marrow disease); the platelet count alone does not tell them apart.
There are many causes (blood diseases, blood loss, inflammation, drugs and others) — interpret together with the clinical data.

slides.title: Platelet morphology (Romanowsky–Giemsa)
rows: Round or oval, 3–4 µm across; hyalomere and granulomere clearly distinct
2–3 µm, round, oval or toothed, with scant cytoplasm
Large, elongated, with blue or pink cytoplasm, azurophilic granules, vacuolated

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: The red-cell count per µL of blood must be known beforehand for the calculation — a wrong red-cell count also distorts the platelet count.
The result depends on the quality of the smear and correct staining: it must be even, fixed and stained by Romanowsky–Giemsa (see the smear preparation and staining protocol).
Compare with other methods (Goryaev chamber, automatic analyser) and repeat if the discrepancy is large.
Capillary blood may be used to determine the platelet count (see the blood collection protocol for haemostasis).

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Capillary blood from the finger is taken only with sterile materials and single-use scarifiers.
Work in rubber gloves; never pipette by mouth with a glass pipette.
Used scarifiers, capillaries and slides are disinfected and put into a puncture-proof container.
